analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations, like lighter duty or bathroom breaks, for pregnant workers.
analysis.headline: A bill to protect pregnant workers from being forced off the job drew 113 House supporters, all Democrats, but never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act would have made it illegal for employers to refuse reasonable accommodations to workers whose pregnancies limit their ability to do certain job tasks, like lifting, standing for long shifts, or taking bathroom breaks. Employers could refuse only if the accommodation would impose an 'undue hardship,' the same standard used under the Americans with Disabilities Act. The bill also barred employers from forcing pregnant employees to take leave when a workable accommodation exists, and it gave workers the same enforcement tools and remedies available under the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant workers, especially those in physically demanding, low-wage jobs like retail, food service, warehouse work, and nursing, who today are often pushed onto unpaid leave, denied modified duties, or pushed out of their jobs when they ask for a stool, a water bottle, or a lighter lifting limit. Roughly three-quarters of women who work while pregnant are in the workforce into their third trimester, and many cannot afford unpaid leave. The bill would also protect applicants denied jobs because they might need an accommodation, and it covers employees of Congress itself, federal offices, and state employees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pregnant workers in physically demanding jobs

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to make reasonable accommodations to known limitations related to pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions, unless the employer can show an undue hardship on its business operations [S2][S3].

Bars employers from denying job opportunities based on the need to make such accommodations, from forcing workers to accept an unwanted accommodation, and from forcing employees to take leave when another reasonable accommodation would work [S2][S3].

Gives workers enforcement powers, procedures, and remedies — including attorneys' fees and damages — through the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the courts, modeled on Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and prohibits retaliation against anyone who asserts these rights [S3].

Directs the EEOC to issue regulations within two years identifying specific reasonable accommodations that employers must provide, and defines 'reasonable accommodation' and 'undue hardship' by the standards courts already use under the Americans with Disabilities Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost of accommodations — light duty, modified schedules, equipment, additional breaks — and of defending themselves against complaints. Most accommodations for pregnancy are inexpensive, but employers in industries built around fixed physical demands and tight staffing would face real adjustments. Small businesses with limited flexibility would bear proportionally larger burdens, and the bill allows lawsuits with damages for violations.

drawbacks.text: Employers would bear the cost of accommodations and litigation, and small businesses with little scheduling flexibility or thin margins would find some adjustments hardest to absorb [S2].

The undue-hardship defense mirrors the Americans with Disabilities Act standard, which businesses argue is still costly and unpredictable, and the bill directs the EEOC to write new regulations that could impose compliance burdens on employers nationwide [S3].

Critics of similar measures have argued that requiring accommodations could make some employers hesitant to hire pregnant applicants, an effect the bill attempts to counter by making denial of employment based on accommodation needs itself unlawful [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address a concrete, common harm: pregnant workers in physically demanding jobs losing income or employment over inexpensive accommodations. The employer-side costs are real but constrained — the bill keeps the familiar ADA 'undue hardship' standard, so accommodations that genuinely threaten a business's operation can be refused. The main design trade-off is enforcement through individual lawsuits and EEOC regulations, which creates compliance uncertainty for employers rather than a bright-line rule. On balance, the burden falls mainly on employers in exchange for protecting workers' health and income during pregnancy.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to four committees, then to subcommittees, and it sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act on May 8, 2012, joined by 66 original cosponsors including Reps. Carolyn Maloney, George Miller, and Rosa DeLauro [S3].

The bill was referred to four House committees — Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary — with consideration to be determined later [S1][S5].

On May 18, 2012 it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution, and on September 26, 2012 to the Education and the Workforce Committee's Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions [S5].

The bill accumulated 112 cosponsors, all Democrats, plus the sponsor, but no committee ever reported it and the House never voted on it before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4][S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — particularly those in physically demanding, low-wage industries — remained free to require pregnant workers to take unpaid leave, refuse modified duties, or push them out, with no federal accommodation requirement and no liability. Workers gained nothing from this outcome; the same protections only became federal law a decade later, in 2022.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who faced no accommodation requirement

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 66 original cosponsors

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee leadership
against.role: Panel of primary referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, letting it die in committee without a hearing

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and calendar
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor and referred it to four committees at once, a path that made single-track consideration unlikely

sides.party_line_note: All 113 supporters — the sponsor and 112 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; Republicans held the House majority, and the bill never advanced in committee or on the floor [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers, especially retail, food service, warehousing, and other physically demanding industries
industries.note: These employers would have been required to provide modest accommodations — stools, water, lighter lifting limits, schedule changes — instead of pushing pregnant workers onto unpaid leave or out the door. Keeping the current system in place preserves their staffing flexibility and shifts the cost of pregnancy onto the workers themselves.

Small employers would bear the same accommodation duty with less scheduling slack, though the bill lets them refuse accommodations that impose an undue hardship and phases in EEOC regulations over two years.
